opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that the way we've pre-trained models so far was really optimized for a particular kind of capability: predicting the next token on a huge corpus of mostly static text from the internet. That gets you remarkable fluency, a lot of world knowledge, and surprisingly good reasoning in short bursts. But an agent has to do something quite different. It has to take actions over long horizons, observe the consequences, recover from mistakes, and keep track of a goal across many steps, sometimes across hours of interaction with tools, codebases, or environments.

If you look at the pre-training data, very little of it actually looks like that. The internet is mostly the *outputs* of human work, the finished essay, the final version of the code, not the messy process of getting there: the trial and error, the debugging, the "I tried this, it failed, so I'll go back and try something else." So we end up asking post-training, fine-tuning and RL, to teach behaviors the base model has almost no prior for. Post-training is very good at eliciting and shaping capabilities already latent in the model. It's much less good at creating them from scratch.

So when I say rethinking pre-training from fundamentals, I mean asking a few questions again. What data mixture actually builds the right priors for agentic behavior? How do we represent long-horizon interaction and feedback during pre-training rather than bolting it on at the end? What objectives besides next-token prediction encourage planning and self-correction? And on the systems side, how do context length, memory, and efficient inference interact with all of that, since agents consume and generate far more tokens than a single chat turn?

Having worked on large-scale pre-training like PaLM, I saw how much of the downstream capability gets baked in at that stage. My view is that if we want agents that are reliable rather than impressive in demos and brittle in practice, we can't treat pre-training as a solved, frozen step. We have to design it with agency as a first-class goal from the start.

r001.rationale: The response says agents must take actions, observe consequences, and interact with tools, codebases, or environments over many steps.

r002.rationale: It says post-training is less able to create capabilities from scratch and that the base model has little prior for agentic behavior.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention whether benchmarks for measuring agentic intelligence exist.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the short version is that the way we've pre-trained models for the last several years was optimized for a very different objective than what agents actually need to do.

Think about what next-token prediction on web text rewards. It rewards being a good one-shot predictor. You see a context, you produce the most plausible continuation, and you get graded on that single step. That's a great recipe for a model that can write an essay or answer a question. But an agent isn't doing one step. It's doing fifty or five hundred steps, and the thing that matters is whether the whole trajectory lands somewhere useful. Errors compound. A model that's ninety-five percent reliable per step is almost useless at step forty, because the probability you've gone off the rails is enormous by then.

And the usual answer has been, fine, we'll fix that in post-training. We'll do some supervised fine-tuning on agent traces, we'll do RL with tool use, and we'll bolt on the agentic behavior at the end. My experience is that this works up to a point and then you hit a wall, because you're fighting the prior. The base model has internalized a worldview where text is static, where it never gets feedback from the environment, where it never has to decide what to do when the thing it just tried didn't work. You can push against that with RL, but you're spending a lot of compute to unlearn something you baked in during the most expensive phase of training.

So the question I keep coming back to is, what if the pre-training data and objective reflected the actual structure of the task? What does it look like to pre-train on interaction rather than just observation? That means data where there's a notion of state, of actions that change the state, of outcomes you observe after acting. It means caring about things like calibration and knowing when to stop and ask, because an agent that confidently plows ahead is much worse than one that says, I'm not sure, let me check. And it means thinking about long-horizon credit assignment as a first-class concern, not something you patch in later.

There's also a more basic data question. The web is a record of what people wrote, not a record of what people did. Most of the actual process of getting something done, the dead ends, the debugging, the "that didn't work, try this instead," never gets written down. The polished artifact survives and the trajectory that produced it doesn't. So we've trained models on the answers without the work, and then we're surprised when they struggle to do the work.

I don't think this means throwing out everything we know. Scale still matters, the transformer still works. But I do think the field got a little complacent, treating pre-training as a solved problem and putting all the creativity into post-training. If you want agents that are actually reliable in the world, I think you have to go back and ask what the model should be learning from the very beginning.

r001.rationale: The response says useful agents need pre-training on interaction, including state, actions that change state, and outcomes observed after acting.

r002.rationale: It says supervised fine-tuning and RL can help only up to a point, then hit a wall, and argues agent capabilities should be addressed during pre-training.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention whether benchmarks for measuring agentic intelligence exist.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental question is: what are we training the model to do, and how does that relate to what we expect an agent to do? In pre-training, we typically ask a model to predict the next token. That gives us a very powerful foundation for language, knowledge, and even reasoning. But an agent needs to take actions, observe what happened, and adapt over multiple steps toward a goal.

That introduces a different kind of learning problem. The next plausible response isn’t necessarily the action that makes progress. An agent may need to ask for clarification, use a tool, or recognize that its previous approach failed. And the consequences of a decision might only become clear much later.

So rethinking pre-training means looking at the data, the objectives, and the kinds of experience the model learns from. Are we learning only from descriptions of completed tasks, or also from interaction, feedback, and recovery from mistakes? How do we build a foundation that makes those capabilities easier to learn?

Post-training is still essential. But if we want agents that generalize reliably to new situations, I think we have to examine the whole training process, starting with the fundamentals.

r001.rationale: The response says an agent must take actions, observe outcomes, and adapt over multiple steps, and asks about learning from interaction and feedback.

r002.rationale: It says post-training is essential but argues that reliable agents require examining the whole training process, starting with fundamentals, communicating that post-training alone is insufficient.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention that benchmarks for measuring agentic intelligence may not yet exist.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it starts with asking what we want an agent to learn. In pre-training, we typically ask a model to predict the next token from a sequence. That gives us a very powerful foundation, but an agent needs to do more: choose an action, observe what happens, and adapt its behavior toward a goal over multiple steps.

So the fundamental question is: how do we connect the learning objective to that process? What should the training data look like? What feedback does the model receive? And how does it learn that an action which looks reasonable locally might lead to a bad outcome several steps later?

Language is still incredibly useful, but we need to think about learning from interaction as well as learning from descriptions of interaction. If we want agents that can recover from mistakes and operate reliably, those capabilities need to inform how we build the foundation, alongside what we do in post-training.

r001.rationale: It says agents must choose actions, observe outcomes, adapt toward goals, and learn from interaction.

r002.rationale: It says agent capabilities must inform foundation-building alongside post-training, indicating post-training alone is insufficient.

r003.rationale: It does not mention whether benchmarks for measuring agentic intelligence exist.
